wbg_operations.title: Kenya Secondary Education Equity and Quality Improvement Program
wbg_operations.amount_basis: World Bank original commitment (USD), whole operation; not allocated to clusters
wbg_operations.description: This Operation Information Summary (OIS) outlines a proposal for a new operation focused on secondary education (Junior, and Secondary Education). The proposed operation builds on the ongoing objectives and interventions under the Kenya Secondary Education Quality Improvement Project (SEQIP P160083), and Kenya: Primary Education Equity in Learning Program (KPLEEP, P176867) operations, to further consolidate, at scale, promising interventions. The proposed operation will use the financing instrument, a Program for Results (PforR), to complement KPEELP Program’s objectives by emphasizing result-oriented strategies, systems strengthening and capacity building of relevant oversight institutions to improve overall policy implementation, and equitable service delivery.Context Summary The basic education system needs to expand rapidly to accommodate the nearly 2 million students expected to enroll in Junior and Senior Schools over the next 7 years. Of immediate concern is the 1.7 Million in Junior school, grade 7, that will join Grade 9 in about 18 months (January 2025). These learners will require an additional 20,000 new classrooms nationwide. The government has put in place fiscal measures to recruit an additional 120,000 teachers for junior and senior by 2025, and instructional materials are being developed from November 2023 for grade 9. Overall, from 2010 to 2022, enrollment in secondary education grew at an average of 7 percent per year, increasing from 1.6 million to 3.8 million students.   However, transition rates have yet to reach their pre-pandemic peak of 91.0 percent in 2020, as they dropped to 78.5 in 2021 due to the pandemic and remained around 78.6 in 2022.  Maintaining the growing demand and the recovery has demanded significant resources and Kenya has consistently invested around 5 percent of its GDP during the last decade. Sustaining the high levels of investment to address growing needs in education is therefore a necessity. At the same time, Kenya has made immense efforts in the roll out of the Competency Based Curriculum (CBC) and Competency Based Assessment (CBA). The Presidential Working party on Education Reforms (PWPER, 2022/2023) recently conducted an evaluation of the implementation of the CBC and CBA in the past 4-5 years and has made solid technical recommendations to further improve implementation of the CBC and CBA. The  emerging challenges in the PWPER report include a need to further  redefine the scope and learning areas of the CBC to focus better on core competencies only; align teacher preparation and support at the school level to new pedagogical approaches required for the CBC and CBA; provision of operational costs and  a minimum essential package of school inputs for adequate implementation of the CBC and CBA, and to minimize demands on parents/households on CBC related costs for each learner; and  establishment of a robust monitoring and learning process for the CBC and CBA to continuously inform improvements and adjustments. The expansion and roll-out of CBC and CBA will need to deliberately address existing inequalities in access and learning in order to improve learning outcomes for all children. Regarding access, although the national gross enrollment rate in secondary stood at 76.5 percent, 9 counties presented rates under 40 percent.  Poorer educational outcomes are also concentrated in the poorest populations and some counties in the north and northeast. Similarly, while gender parity has been achieved in access at a national level, disparities in learning outcomes remain significant: on average, girls underperform in math and science at both primary and secondary national  tests. In addition, improving learning outcomes in secondary education in rural areas, lagging regions and for poorer populations is essential to achieve the objectives Kenya has set for itself, in improving education performance, including school to work transition. Proposed Results AreasThe proposed PforR program will support the implementation of a series of recommendations in three focus areas: i) expanding equitable access to quality Junior and Senior School Education; ii) Further transformation of teaching and teacher management and support and; iii) Systems strengthening and building institutional capacity for equitable service delivery, fostering inclusivity and equality. These focus areas are aligned to the National Education Sector Strategy and Plan (NESSP II) as well as the PWPER report recommendations specifically concerning junior and senior schools Education. Below is a preliminary scoping of the proposed Results Areas for the new operation: a)	Result Area 1: Expanding Equitable Access to Quality Junior and Senior School Education: i.	Adequate implementation and monitoring of CBC and CBA in Junior and Senior Schools:  Develop an operational plan with critical milestones and timelines for implementation of the CBC and CBA in Junior and Secondary Schools, implement the proposed reforms in e-assessments under the CBA, and develop and implement robust monitoring and learning mechanisms for CBC and CBA implementation to inform continuous improvements in implementation. ii.	Infrastructure Development: Construction of new 20,000 classrooms/integrated learning resource centers for Junior School, and the associated WASH facilities to meet the WASH-students ratio standards for Junior schools. Regarding the National school meals program, infrastructure development will also include construction of kitchen/food safety facilities as needed, clean cooking energy, and fencing of schools particularly where children are considered exposed and vulnerable. iii.	Inclusive Education: Specific efforts to improve performance of girls’ and vulnerable boys’ performance in Sciences, Mathematics and English (SME); in Special Needs Education (SNE), strengthen data quality to inform targeting and investments for various SNE categories, and capacity building of 10 regional Educational Assessment Centers; and support development of guidelines for accelerated learning and implementation of these guidelines targeting marginalized learners and out-of-school children and youth, and the enhancing of adult and continuing education. b)	Result Area 2: Further Transformation of the Teaching Quality, Teacher Development and Management.  i.	Enhance quality and relevance of Pre-service and in-service teaching training interventions.  Further support the development and implementation of teaching training programs and retooling activities, alignment to Competency-Based Teacher Education (CBTE) and Competency-Based Teacher Assessment (CBTA) for Junior and Senior Schools. ii.	Enhancing provision of high quality and affordable instructional materials: Support the implementation of reforms for instructional materials under the School Learning and Instructional Material Centre (SLIMC), for CBC and CBA, including teachers’ resources, mobile science kits for Junior school, virtual labs for Senior School, and adapted instructional materials and learning assistive devices for learners with Special Needs Education (SNE). iii.	Technology integration for remote learning: Scaling up virtual teaching/live streaming in schools affected by teacher physical presence mainly due to insecurity. An independent of the live streaming pilot is initiated to inform design for the scale up. c)	Results Area 3: Systems Strengthening and Building Institutional Capacity for Equitable Service Delivery.Building systems and enhancing institutional capacity and quality to improve equitable service delivery in a systemic and sustainable approach. Relevant institutional assessments will be conducted to inform strategic systems strengthening and capacity building: i.  Enhancing a Central Scholarship Administration System at the Jomo Kenyatta Foundation (JKF). Centralizing the fragmented offer of scholarships by various financing sources with improved targeting to further increase transparency and reach
iati_titles: Kenya Secondary Education Equity and Quality Improvement Program

wbg_operations.title: First Somalia Economic Resilience Development Policy Financing
wbg_operations.amount_basis: World Bank original commitment (USD), whole operation; not allocated to clusters
wbg_operations.sector: Agriculture, Fishing and Forestry,Energy and Mineral Resources,Financial Sector,Public Administration
wbg_operations.description: The development objective of the First Somalia Economic Resilience Development Policy Financing for Somalia is to promote economic resilience through more sustainable public finances and resilient private sector development. Pillar A aims to ensure sustainable public finances. This will contribute to the macroeconomic stability and will expand fiscal space required to meet Somalia’s large development needs in the context of high volatility to climate change and fragility, conflict, and violence. Pillar B aims to enable resilient private sector development. This pillar supports structural reforms that enhance the environment for private-sector-led growth and create conditions for job creation, increasing the resilience of households.

wbg_operations.title: Innovative Systems to Promote Integrated, Resilient and Enhanced Responses to Women and Girls’ Health
wbg_operations.amount_basis: World Bank original commitment (USD), whole operation; not allocated to clusters
wbg_operations.description:
The objective of the Innovative Systems to Promote Integrated, Resilient, and Enhanced Responses to Women and Girls’ Health Project for Ethiopia is to improve women and girls’ health outcomes and strengthen health systems in climate-stressed areas. The project has four components. (1) Expand access to quality interventions for women and girls, including through tech-enabled care component will develop and implement a system-based cervical cancer prevention program using a community-based, digitally supported service delivery platform; Enhance HEWs capacity to provide quality care by establishing digital learning platforms for continuing education, performance management and certification of skill development, and
capacity building to deliver basic preventive and promotive healthcare services for women and girls; Enhance service delivery availability and efficiency by purchasing and introducing portable AIenabled ultrasound machines for 500 healthcare centers; and Implement m-mama emergency response system by improving remote triage implementing a digitalized dispatch system, tracking patient outcomes using public ambulance and private taxi ambulances using the m-mama experience. (2) Improve service delivery through innovative interventions in climate-stressed and conflict-affected areas component will: provide renewable solar energy for 500 healthcare centers to provide adequate lighting in delivery rooms to enable safe nighttime deliveries for continuous service provision and avoid unnecessary referrals; implement waterless toilet technologies to improve WASH systems of 240 healthcare facilities in climate-stressed and water-scarce areas with high patient volumes; implement innovative environmental technology (Ecosterly) for medical waste management in four hospitals to support medical waste treatment and recycling; revise minimum design requirements for healthcare facility construction and renovation standards to include alternative renewable energy sources, digital connectivity standards, and materials to ensure facility resilience in times of climate-related shocks. (3) Strengthen data systems and reinforce decision-making to ensure high-quality care component will uild institutional capacity to implement health sector innovations, including integration of data generated through project-supported innovations; Improve decision-making capacity in big data analytics, modeling, and proactive surveillance using metrological, environmental, and public health data to predict the impact of climate change and design innovative solutions. (4) Project implementation and monitoring component will provide program management and implementation monitoring support, including supportive supervision of regional health bureaus (RHBs) and implementing entities, conduct mid-term and endline evaluations of implementation of innovative interventions that the project supports, including an impact evaluation of the m-mama emergency response, and omplement key innovations and sector reforms to address lingering women and girls’ health problems and accelerate progress toward the Sustainable Development Goals.
iati_titles: Innovative Systems to Promote Integrated, Resilient and Enhanced Responses to Women and Girls Health

wbg_operations.title: Second Somalia Economic Resilience Development Policy Financing
wbg_operations.amount_basis: World Bank original commitment (USD), whole operation; not allocated to clusters
wbg_operations.sector: Agriculture, Fishing and Forestry,Digital Development,Energy and Mineral Resources,Financial Sector,Public Administration
wbg_operations.description: The Federal Government of Somalia (FGS) was established in 2012 and has implemented important state- and institution-building reforms. Limited state presence and insecurity have weakened the effectiveness of reforms. Furthermore, an unfinished political settlement regarding resource distribution and functional responsibilities among the FGS, the Federal Member States (FMSs), and local authorities has exacerbated this issue. Institutional capacity is gradually improving, supported by the international community, but remains insufficient to deal with the multiple challenges facing Somalia and ensure effective coordination with FMSs on policy design and reform implementation. Continuing conflict hinders growth prospects, limits revenue mobilization, and contributes to high security costs. Federal and state governments collect minimal revenue, despite moderate economic growth over the last several years. The public sector, therefore, has little fiscal space for investments that would generate economic growth and reduce poverty. The reforms supported in this operation complement the World Bank’s engagement in Somalia. The Second Development Policy Financing (DPF 2) is part of the World Bank’s support to help Somalia construct a more stable and legitimate state, foster inclusive private-sector-led growth, and enhance resilience to rebuild the social contract and emerge from FCV. Furthermore, this operation is aligned with corporate commitments on climate co-benefits, reducing gender gaps, maximizing finance for development, and supporting Somalia’s transition out of fragility.
iati_titles: Second Somalia Economic Resilience Development Policy Financing

wbg_operations.title: Ethiopia: Climate Resilient Irrigation for Sustainable Production (CRISP)
wbg_operations.amount_basis: World Bank original commitment (USD), whole operation; not allocated to clusters
wbg_operations.sector: Agriculture, Fishing and Forestry,Industry, Trade and Services
wbg_operations.description: The CRISP project aims to improve access to resilient irrigation services in selected areas of Ethiopia. The project will strengthen the performance, reliability, and climate resilience of irrigation systems by rehabilitating and modernizing key large- and medium-scale schemes, upgrading irrigation infrastructure down to on-farm systems, and expanding small-scale irrigation in vulnerable and food-insecure areas. It will introduce climate-smart and energy-efficient technologies to enhance water-use efficiency and sustainability, and pilot innovative approaches such as irrigation service fee systems, private service provision, water allocation and monitoring mechanisms, and salinity management practices. The project will further support agricultural production and value chain development by improving farmers’ access to inputs, mechanization, and markets, and by strengthening agri-business linkages to increase productivity and incomes. It will promote inclusive and participatory management models, empower water user associations and female farmers, and foster private sector engagement in irrigation services, financing, and agricultural commercialization. In addition, the project will establish digital tools for national irrigation information and asset management, enhance dam safety and environmental and social risk management, and build institutional and technical capacity at federal and regional levels to sustain climate-resilient irrigation development.
iati_titles: Ethiopia: Climate Resilient Irrigation for Sustainable Production (CRISP)

wbg_operations.title: Somalia Disaster Risk Management DPF with a Catastrophe Deferred Draw Down Option
wbg_operations.amount_basis: World Bank original commitment (USD), whole operation; not allocated to clusters
wbg_operations.sector: Agriculture, Fishing and Forestry,Public Administration,Social Protection
wbg_operations.description: The development objective of Disaster Risk Management Development Policy Financing with a Catastrophe Deferred Draw Down Option Project for Somalia is to support the Federal Government of Somalia's (FGS) reform program to improve the country’s institutional, regulatory and response and preparedness capacity to manage climate and disaster risks. After a series of restructures and moves, the Somalia Disaster Management Agency (SoDMA) has become the focal point for the federal government on disaster preparedness and response. The most recent comprehensive assessment of Somalia’s Emergency Preparedness and Response (EP&R) capacity, released in 2022, offered a sobering view of the country’s readiness for disaster. The evolution of the World Bank’s DRM portfolio in Somalia reflects a phased and programmatic approach. Through these engagements over nearly a decade, the government has made significant progress in advancing policy and institutional foundations for DRM. The operation is aligned with the World Bank’s Country Partnership Framework (CPF) (FY24–FY28). The DPF with Cat DDO is also in line with the World Bank Gender Strategy 2024-2030. This operation aligns with the goals of the Paris Agreement. This operation builds on lessons emerging from DPFs prepared in FCV contexts. An Independent Evaluation Group report on engaging with fragile states highlights the importance of focusing on politically feasible reforms that can build momentum for future changes, with an emphasis on restoring and strengthening basic state functions. To balance the need to implement durable policy changes, accompanying institutional reforms and technical assistance are also in place, with close links to IPFs and IFC advisory support. The reforms target areas where there is ongoing collaboration with government counterparts and development partners, which helps ensure complementarity and coordination of efforts.
iati_titles: Somalia Disaster Risk Management DPF with a Catastrophe Deferred Draw Down Option

wbg_operations.title: Kenya Watershed Services Improvement Project
wbg_operations.amount_basis: World Bank original commitment (USD), whole operation; not allocated to clusters
wbg_operations.sector: Agriculture, Fishing and Forestry,Water, Sanitation and Waste Management
wbg_operations.description: Kenya Watershed Services Improvement Project for Kenya has the development objectives to expand the area under sustainable land and watershed management and to improve livelihoods of communities in the project areas. Component 1: Roots of Resilience: Policy, Legal, and Regulatory Framework strengthens the foundation for programmatic and sustained investments in sustainable land and water management by enhancing policy, regulatory, and institutional frameworks, coordination mechanisms, and informed decision-making. Sub-components include Sub-component 1a, which strengthens watershed management institutions and governance by supporting implementation of national restoration strategies, preparing integrated landscape and watershed management plans aligned with county plans, building capacity of county committees, developing local guidelines and investment prioritization tools, reviewing and updating forestry and related regulations, and preparing a Community Grants Manual; Sub-component 1b, which develops and rolls out an integrated watershed and landscape restoration monitoring system through an integrated data-sharing framework, information and communication technology upgrades, laboratory and field equipment, and knowledge management and capacity building at national, county, and community levels; and Sub-component 1c, which establishes sustainable financing mechanisms and investments for watersheds and landscapes, including development of a national Payment for Ecosystem Services (PES) framework, design of benefit-sharing schemes, and incentives and award programs to recognize and scale good practices. Component 2: Green Horizons: Sustainable Landscape and Watershed Management restores and manages degraded landscapes in selected hydrosheds using participatory planning, integrated watershed management plans, and a data-driven investment prioritization tool, while building resilient and diversified livelihoods, with a focus on vulnerable communities. Sub-components include Sub-component 2a, which supports sustainable landscape and watershed management on private and community lands through soil and water conservation measures, small-scale water harvesting, gully rehabilitation, restoration of green corridors for ecological connectivity, area closures with assisted natural regeneration, establishment of woodlots, agroforestry and value addition for high-value tree crops and gums and resins, enrichment of degraded pastures and rangelands, control and management of invasive species, and dedicated grants for minority and marginalized groups to restore natural resource bases and develop enterprises; and Sub-component 2b, which restores gazetted forests by enhancing seed collection, testing, and distribution, expanding nursery capacity and planting for reforestation and natural regeneration, strengthening pest and disease management systems, improving fire surveillance, preparedness and response, controlling invasive species, mapping investment opportunities, and piloting private sector engagement in selected forest blocks. Component 3: Project Management, Training, and Capacity Building consolidates planning, budgeting, implementation, fiduciary management, environmental and social standards compliance, and reporting, and finances the establishment and operation of national and county project structures, monitoring and evaluation, procurement of vehicles and equipment, and targeted capacity building for project staff on procurement, budgeting, reporting, and activity monitoring.
iati_titles: Kenya Watershed Services Improvement Project

wbg_operations.title: Second Community Action for Landscape Management Program for Results
wbg_operations.amount_basis: World Bank original commitment (USD), whole operation; not allocated to clusters
wbg_operations.sector: Agriculture, Fishing and Forestry,Digital Development,Water, Sanitation and Waste Management
wbg_operations.description: This hybrid operation—combining Program-for-Results (PforR) and Investment Project Financing (IPF)—supports the National Strategic Investment Framework for Sustainable Landscape Management (ESIF 2, 2024–2038) by advancing long-term landscape restoration. It aims to: (i) expand sustainable land management in degraded Highland Areas; (ii) sustain and expand certification, registration, and digitalization of rural land rights in Ethiopia’s highlands, including communal forests and grazing lands; and (iii) raise farm incomes and create jobs by strengthening agribusiness value-chain linkages. Primary beneficiaries are smallholder farmers in program watersheds. The program will increase smallholders’ livelihood security and broaden income earning opportunities. Efforts will be made for the equitable inclusion of all beneficiaries in Community Watershed Users’ Cooperative Societies (CWUCS) including vulnerable groups such as landless, youth, elderly, and female-headed households.The PforR component will finance watershed-level sustainable land and natural resource management, strengthen rural land administration, improve tenure security for private and communal lands (including selected forests and grazing areas), and catalyze private-sector participation to ensure sustainability. Under Result Area 1 (Participatory Watershed and Forest Management), Disbursement-Linked Indicators (DLIs) incentivize scaling up restoration and market linkages by: (1) registering Community Watershed Users’ Cooperative Societies (CWUCS) with participatory, approved Watershed Management Plans; (2) expanding the area under sustainable landscape management; (3) establishing Participatory Forest Management with legally recognized cooperatives and approved Forest Management Plans; (4) treating acid soils; (5) integrating cooperatives into existing and new value chains within program catchments; and (6) verifying non forest emission reductions. Under Result Area 2 (Rural Land Administration), DLIs focus on expanding and digitizing secure tenure by: (1) issuing Second Level Land Holding Certificates (SLLCs) for individual parcels; (2) issuing SLLCs for communal forests and grazing lands; (3) operationalizing the National Rural Land Administration Information System in program woredas with digitized SLLCs; and (4) increasing connectivity of land administration offices and systems to national digital infrastructure. The IPF component—financed by IDA, SCALE, Nordic Development Fund (NDF), and ENABLE—will provide cross-cutting technical assistance and capacity building across both result areas and the broader government program (ESIF 2). It will support: (i) agribusiness development by linking landholders to agribusinesses; (ii) design and implementation of payment for ecosystem services (PES) schemes; (iii) access to carbon markets; and (iv) Operationalize pilots to promote voluntary land consolidation in Ethiopia’s highlands. These pilots involve baseline surveys, voluntary land exchange, and design, testing, and documentation of a computerized platform in real-world conditions. The likelihood and magnitude of risk for the voluntary exchange program pilot have been assessed. The voluntary land exchange will take place in 12 designated kebeles, involving small parcels of land and following a national legal proclamation.Targeted TA will also promote inclusive alternative livelihoods for women and youth through group-based training and livelihood grants; strengthen community capacity to scale ecosystem conservation and carbon sequestration via participatory forest and watershed management; advance land tenure and property rights awareness; and establish community-based performance monitoring. In addition, the operation will enhance MoA and Ethiopia Forest Development (EFD) operational capacity for CALM 2, including: (i) environmental and social risk management; (ii) procurement and financial management; and (iii) monitoring, reporting, and verification, including advanced remote sensing. IFC will complement implementation with integrated upstream and downstream support for agribusiness linkages, value-chain development, and access to finance, strengthening market access and supply chains through its portfolio, pipeline, and early-stage leads. IFC’s approach will promote business models that directly engage smallholder farmers and local communities, with close IFC– World Bank collaboration to ensure coordinated delivery.

wbg_operations.title: Housing Finance, Lands and Sustainable Investments
wbg_operations.amount_basis: World Bank original commitment (USD), whole operation; not allocated to clusters
wbg_operations.description: The earlier Kenya Affordable Housing Finance Project (KAHFP) (P165034) made significant strides in expanding access to affordable housing finance in Kenya, primarily through the support and operationalization of the Kenya Mortgage Refinance Company (KMRC). As of December 2025, KMRC refinanced approximately KES 25.3 billion in mortgages, representing 5,148 loans. Repayment tenor lengthened from 8.3 (2021) to 12.3 years (2025) signaling enhanced affordability. Notably, nearly 48 percent of KMRC-refinanced mortgages were issued to women, highlighting significant progress in gender inclusion. KMRC’s portfolio now accounts for about 5.0 percent of the banking sector’s mortgage book by value and 12.8 percent by number of loans. Additionally, the share of refinancing through SACCOs within KMRC’s portfolio grew from 7 percent in 2022 to 15.2 percent by December 2025, indicating a strengthened role for non-bank lenders in the affordable housing finance sector and growing financial inclusion. These achievements demonstrate that KMRC is actively driving the market forward in a positive direction; however, affordability remains a binding constraint for the majority. The Housing Finance, Lands and Sustainable Investments Project - is aimed at strengthening the Kenyan housing market by addressing some of the lingering demand and supply gaps in the sector. To ensure continuity, it proposes to support KMRC with a line of credit for mortgage refinancing, blended with KMRC’s own funding raised through bond issuances on the capital markets, to ensure leverage of the IDA/IBRD resources and the overall sustainability of the mortgage market. The project will aim to deliver additionality by moving beyond conventional mortgage financing and exploring more innovative products that can reach underserved segments of the market. It will also support the State Department of Lands and Physical Planning (SDLPP) in its reforms to make property registration faster, cheaper and more reliable, which is a precondition to develop the mortgage market. Additionally, the project proposes to support the Government of Kenya (GoK), via the National Treasury (NT), in launching a sovereign sustainability-linked loan (SLL). The innovative instrument ties the cost of borrowing to national sustainability targets, aligning Kenya’s financing needs with measurable environmental and development outcomes that would also have co-benefits for housing. It will also support a sub-sovereign sustainability bond issuance by KMRC.The four components of the project include: Component 1: Support to KMRC. This component will provide a line of credit to KMRC and ensure continuity and enhanced uptake of the company’s current product offering while innovating to serve unmet market needs. IBRD will provide a credit line to KMRC through the NT to refinance affordable housing loans. As in the first phase of the project, KMRC will extend loans to banks and Savings and Credit Cooperative Organizations (SACCOs) collectively known as Primary Mortgage Lenders (PMLs) that meet strict eligibility criteria. Such loans will be secured against eligible mortgage/housing loans. Moving beyond conventional mortgage financing, KMRC will pilot innovative refinancing products tailored to underserved market segments. These offerings will include microloans, incremental construction lending, and green mortgages and are designed to address affordability, informality, and climate resilience gaps.Component 2: Support to land administration reforms to accelerate affordable housing. This component would support the State Department of Lands and Physical Planning (SDLPP) in its reforms to make property registration faster, cheaper and more reliable, which is a precondition to develop the mortgage market. Building off the technical assistance completed under KAFHP 1, the Project support will be structured into three sub-components: (2.1) enabling the environment for property and mortgage registration through legal and regulatory reforms: supporting the SDLPP to review, harmonize, and enact legislation to support end-to-end digital land transactions and promote consistency across land administration statutes; (2.2) digitization of spatial and land records data, including geodetic improvements: digitizing existing property rights data (titles, deeds, transfer documents, etc.) and graphical spatial data (survey plans, etc.) so that it is fully available in the digital system; and (2.3) enhancing the Ardhisasa land administration management system by addressing systemic issues: improving the system via business process reengineering to simplify processes, enhance automatic data checks, e-signature and other functionality.Component 3: Sustainable Financing Instruments. Subcomponent 3.1: Sovereign Sustainability-Linked Loan involves the development and issuance of a sovereign Sustainability Linked Loan (SLL) program, to leverage the GoK's strong sustainability agenda to diversify investors and access more affordable international capital. Sovereign borrowing in Kenya has been costly, making innovative financing tools such as this more attractive.  Subcomponent 3.2: Sustainability Bond Issuance. Building on the robust framework and market precedent set by sovereign, KMRC is preparing for its inaugural sustainability bond issuance. This approach will enable KMRC to attract a diverse pool of investors and enhance market credibility. The transition to sustainability bonds will also support KMRC’s commitment to environmental and social impact, further strengthening its role in Kenya’s financial ecosystem. The World Bank financing will provide credit enhancements for the sovereign and sub-sovereign issuances.Component 4: Technical Assistance and Project Management: The TA will support Component 1 and overall project management. Activities will cover the development of new product offerings and assess market readiness. It will help define product characteristics and support the development and implementation of roll out plans. The TA will also help operationalize the Kenya Mortgage Guarantee Trust (KMGT), including capacity building and procurement of relevant IT systems. Additionally, the TA will support preparations for future bond issuances through transaction advisory services and consultancy support. This component will also finance project management and related capacity building.

wbg_operations.amount_basis: World Bank original commitment (USD), whole operation; not allocated to clusters
wbg_operations.sector: FY17 - Water, Sanitation and Waste Management
wbg_operations.description: The objective of the Kenya Urban Water and Sanitation OBA Fund for Low-income Areas is to increase the number of people in low income areas with access to improved water supply and sanitation services. This objective will be realized by incentivizing urban WSPs to invest in water supply and sanitation improvement subprojects to benefit households in low income areas by applying one-off OBA subsidies to make water and sanitation access affordable. The components of the project are implementation of support activities, project management, sub-project preparation and supervision and independent verification. This component seeks to ensure effective management of the project in line with the World Bank fiduciary obligations. The second component is OBA subsidies for water and sanitation subprojects. It will provide OBA subsidies for sub-project investments made by WSPs to ensure that low income areas benefit from this expansion and improved services.
iati_titles: Kenya Urban Water and Sanitation OBA Fund for Low Income Areas

wbg_operations.title: Oromia Forested Landscape Program – Emission Reduction Project
wbg_operations.amount_basis: World Bank original commitment (USD), whole operation; not allocated to clusters
wbg_operations.description: The development objective of Oromia Forested Landscape Program - Emission Reduction Project for Ethiopia aims to generate measured, reported and verified Emissions Reductions (ER) from reduced deforestation, forest degradation, enhancement of forest carbon stocks (REDD+), agriculture and other land use sectors that meet the Greenhouse Gas (GHG) accounting requirements of the BioCarbon Fund (BioCF) Initiative for Sustainable Forest Landscapes (ISFL) in the Oromia State and will distribute ER payments in accordance with an agreed benefit sharing plan. This project has two components. The first component, Emission Reductions payments distributed in accordance with agreed Benefit Sharing Plan, includes the following sub-components: (i) Payment for Emission Reduction Credits; and (ii) Distribution of ER payments as per a Benefit Sharing Plan (BSP). 2) The second component, Comprehensive Measurement, reporting and verification (MRV) system and program management, including E&S Risk Management system, has the following sub-components: (i) Program Management including E&S standards Implementation and communication; and (ii) Improvement of the Comprehensive Measurement, Reporting and Verification system.
iati_titles: Oromia Forested Landscape Program – Emission Reduction Project

wbg_operations.title: Oromia National Regional State Forested Landscape Program
wbg_operations.amount_basis: World Bank original commitment (USD), whole operation; not allocated to clusters
wbg_operations.description: The development objective of the  Oromia National Regional State Forested Landscape Project for Ethiopia is to improve the enabling environment for sustainable forest managementand investment in Oromia. The project has three components. First component, enabling investments will finance investment in PFM (including livelihoods support and selected nature-based community enterprise development) and reforestation in deforestation hotspots insites to be selected, as well as extension services and land-use planning statewide at state and local levels. Second component, enabling environment will finance complementary activities to improve the effectiveness andimpact of institutions, policies, marketing, BSM, and information (that is, strategiccommunication, MRV), and safeguards management at state and local levels. This component will enhance the enabling environment to help scale up and leverage action on the ground toreduce deforestation and forest degradation. Third component, emission reduction payments will be made only for emission reductions achieved during the ERPA period. However, interventions conducive to emission reductions can start at any time. ER payments will be delivered once results are achieved,verified by a third party, and formally reported to the Bank. In addition, the ER payments will not cover the full cost of implementing changes in landscape management. The ER payments will provide some return that offsets some costs of improving the landscape for the wider benefitof all.
iati_titles: Oromia National Regional State Forested Landscape Program
wbg_operations.geography_scope: Country / regional context; no cluster location established

wbg_operations.title: Second Ethiopia Resilient Landscapes and Livelihoods Project
wbg_operations.amount_basis: World Bank original commitment (USD), whole operation; not allocated to clusters
wbg_operations.sector: FY17 - Agriculture, Fishing and Forestry,FY17 - Industry, Trade and Services,FY17 - Public Administration
wbg_operations.description: The development objective of Second Resilient Landscapes and Livelihoods Project (RLLP II) for Ethiopia to improve climate resilience, land productivity and carbon storage, and increase access to diversified livelihood activities in selected rural watersheds. This project has three components. 1) The first component, Green Infrastructure and Resilient Livelihoods, has the following sub-components: (i) Land Restoration and Watershed Management; (ii) Climate Smart Agriculture; and (iii) Livelihood Diversification and Connections to Value Chains. 2) The second component, Investing in Institutions and Information for Resilience, aims to enhance institutional capacity and improve information for better decision-making in supporting resilient landscapes and diversified rural livelihoods in the project area, both for the duration of the project and after project completion. 3) The third component, Project Management and Reporting, aims to support project management and reporting, including financing of operating costs and implementation of project fiduciary aspects, including financial management, procurement, environmental and social safeguards, and monitoring and evaluation and reporting for the forty-seven watersheds under RLLP II.
iati_titles: Second Ethiopia Resilient Landscapes and Livelihoods Project
wbg_operations.geography_scope: Country / regional context; no cluster location established
